analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks, bonds, and commodities.
analysis.headline: A bill to bar members of Congress and their immediate families from trading individual stocks was introduced in March 2025 with 5 cosponsors and has sat in four House committees without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children to own or trade individual stocks, bonds, commodities, derivatives, hedge fund interests, or other complex investments. They would have to sell existing holdings within 180 days of the law passing (90 days for future members), and could only keep broad, diversified index-type funds, Treasury bonds, government retirement accounts, and similar holdings. Violations would carry civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation, enforced by the Attorney General or the Special Counsel. The bill has been referred to four House committees and has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who cannot trade on nonpublic information gain a government whose lawmakers' finances are not tied to individual company fortunes. Honest members also gain a clear rule instead of ambiguous disclosure-based ethics.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens, and members who follow the rules

how_it_helps.text: Bars members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from owning or trading stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, derivatives, options, and hedge fund or other complex investment vehicles [S2]

Requires current members to divest covered assets within 180 days of enactment, future members within 90 days of taking office, and members who receive assets by inheritance to divest within 180 days [S2]

Allows only widely held, diversified investment funds, Treasury securities, government retirement plan funds, Alaska Native settlement stock, small business interests, and assets tied to a spouse's own occupation [S2]
Authorizes civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, enforceable by the Attorney General or the Special Counsel, without limiting other criminal or civil remedies [S2]
Defers capital gains tax on assets sold to comply with the ban, so members are not taxed as if they sold voluntarily [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would have to sell individual holdings and keep their investments in broad funds or Treasury securities. Asset managers and brokers also lose this niche of wealthy, well-connected individual clients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The main penalty is a civil fine of at most $100,000 per violation, which is small relative to the wealth of many members and could be treated as a cost of doing business [S2]

The exceptions are broad: members may keep assets from a spouse's 'primary occupation,' small business interests, and any fund that is merely 'diversified' and 'does not present a conflict of interest' — terms the ethics committees would define themselves [S2]
The bill gives members a tax break on their own forced sales, deferring capital gains tax on divested assets, a benefit unavailable to ordinary investors [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core ban is strong and would close the most visible conflict-of-interest channel in Congress: trading individual companies while writing laws that affect them. But the enforcement is soft (a modest civil fine, prosecuted at the Justice Department's discretion) and the exceptions leave room for members to keep conflicted assets through a spouse's business or loosely defined funds. The bill would be a real improvement over current law, which requires only disclosure of trades after the fact, but it is not airtight.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four different House committees at once and then to a subcommittee, and since late March 2025 no committee has taken it up, so it has never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the bill on March 6, 2025 [S1]
Five Republican House members cosponsored it; no Democrats are listed as cosponsors [S3]
The Speaker referred it simultaneously to the Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration, and Ways and Means committees, 'for a period to be subsequently determined' [S4]
On March 28, 2025, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development, and no further action has been recorded since [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress, who remain free under current law to trade individual stocks as long as they disclose the trades later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who keep trading rights

for.name: Rep. Tim Burchett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban congressional stock trading and shepherded its introduction

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to a subcommittee on March 28, 2025, and has taken no further recorded action — no markup, hearing, or vote

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to four committees simultaneously, splitting jurisdiction and leaving each committee waiting on the others, with no deadline set

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 5 cosponsors are Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors listed, but no vote has occurred to reveal how the parties would actually split.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and their families
industries.note: The bill would force them to sell individual stocks, bonds, commodities, and hedge fund interests and keep their money in broad funds or Treasury securities, ending their ability to trade companies they regulate and oversee. As long as the bill stalls, they keep the current disclosure-only regime.

Brokers and fund managers would lose a small niche of wealthy congressional clients forced to liquidate, but most of the industry is unaffected; broadly, individual-stock trading by a few hundred families is not a material market segment.

analysis.trajectory: The outlook is poor. Bills sent to multiple committees with only a handful of cosponsors and no committee action after months rarely reach the floor; a ban on members' own trading also needs leadership to prioritize it against the members' personal interest. Comparable proposals in recent Congresses have drawn broad public attention but repeatedly died in committee, and unless a larger coalition or a discharge petition forces action, this bill is likely to end the Congress without a vote.
